Ask for the Latin root and the old reading-aloud practice. Pedagogy dials and camp wars are sibling territory, not this etymology card.

items.why: False either-or. How expert the learner is should dial how much guidance you give.
faces: false dichotomy; the real variable is how expert the learner already is. Guide beginners closely; loosen guidance as skill grows.
A student in a novice coding class gets worked examples first, then freer projects later. Expertise dials how much guidance.
In an adaptive course, strong structure comes early and sandboxes open as prior knowledge grows. Camp wars miss that dial.
The real variable is how expert the learner already is. Guide beginners closely; loosen guidance as skill grows.
Unlike a pure either-or of telling versus discovery forever, the method should track where the learner sits on expertise.
If someone forces a lifelong pick a side, reject the false dichotomy. Ask how much guidance this expertise needs now.
Ask whether guidance matches current skill. Tight for beginners, looser later - not a permanent identity fight.
This is not Kirschner alone restated as a paper cite. It is the false-dichotomy framing: expertise dials the mix.
Give training wheels that come off with skill. Not a lifelong wheels versus no-wheels tribal choice.
Direct instruction versus discovery as a pure forever choice is the wrong fight. Expertise sets the guidance level.
Beginners need close guidance; freer discovery helps more after knowledge is in place. The dial moves with skill.
Decoder: is the stem forcing an eternal camp? Correct move is expertise-sensitive guidance, not a permanent side.
Build sequences that start guided and release into discovery as competence rises. That dial is the claim.
nearMiss: Kirschner-style novice guidance appears in the vignette, yet the framing here is false dichotomy: expertise dials how much guidance, not a lifelong pick-a-side.
Beginners get worked examples; freer sandboxes open later. Same sequencing surface as the 2006 paper, landing on reject eternal telling-versus-discovery camps.
Strong structure early and looser exploration after knowledge grows. The claim is the dial moves with skill, not only citing anti-unguided-for-novices as a paper title.
If someone forces a permanent identity fight between direct instruction and discovery, refuse it. Ask how expert the learner is and set guidance to match now.
Training wheels that come off with competence. Not a tribal forever choice and not reducible to one 2006 citation alone; expertise sets the mix.

items.why: If they have not learned, the instruction has not taught. Fix materials before blaming the student.
faces: if the student has not learned, the instruction has not taught. Treat confusion as a flaw in the teaching materials, not the student.
A student misses the objective and the first redesign targets clearer wording and examples, not try harder as the opening move.
In the online module, the same persistent error across many learners triggers a materials rewrite before aptitude blame.
If they did not learn it, the instruction has not taught. Treat confusion as a flaw in the teaching materials first.
Unlike blaming the learner's effort first, this stance says failed learning means the materials failed to communicate.
If half the class shares the same miss, fix the sequence and examples. Materials carry the failure until proven otherwise.
Ask whether the design assumes the student is the defect. Default here: the instruction failed to teach.
This is not softness about standards. It is accountability on the materials when learning did not occur.
Give a common wrong answer pattern and revise the worksheet before scolding motivation. Materials failed first.
Same stuck point for many students means the explanation or examples broke, not a room full of lazy minds.
Treat non-learning as evidence the communication was not faultless. Redesign the teaching object.
Decoder: did learning fail? Point at instruction and materials first. That is the faultless-communication move.
Build assessment review that starts with what the materials did wrong when the class did not learn.
nearMiss: Scripted choral drills and capital-DI packaging may show up in nearby items, but here failed learning means the instruction has not taught. Fix materials first.
In the online module a shared wrong answer pattern triggers a worksheet rewrite before aptitude blame. Confusion is a flaw in teaching objects, not the student.
Engelmann Direct Instruction scripts are a different card. This stance: if they did not learn it, treat the communication as not faultless and redesign the teaching.
Unlike labeling the branded DI model, default when learning fails is that the materials failed to communicate. Try-harder is not the opening move.
Ask whether the design points at the student as the defect. Default here points at instruction and examples until the materials prove otherwise.

items.term: Lowercase di vs capital-D Direct Instruction
items.why: lowercase di = teacher-led teaching in general; DI = Engelmann and Becker's named scripted program.
faces: di means teacher-led teaching in general; DI means one specific scripted program by Engelmann and Becker. Everyday teacher-led versus that named program.
Scripted choral lessons with tight sequences mark Engelmann-Becker Direct Instruction, not just any teacher talk.
Ask whether the lesson is a published script with signals and unison answers, or merely the instructor explaining from the front.
Unlike lecture-style telling, capital-DI packages every wording, example order, and student response cue.
If the class only hears explanations without a fixed script, that is little-d teacher-led instruction, not Direct Instruction.
This is not the same as standing and talking: DI uses engineered materials with prescribed wording.
Student hears a signal, answers in unison from a scripted frame, then gets immediate correctives on that frame.
Tool check: does the slide pack include exact teacher lines and error corrections, or open-ended lecture notes?
Front-of-room explaining alone never earns the Direct Instruction label used in Module 1.
Decoder: capital D equals scripted Engelmann-Becker program; lowercase equals general teacher-led delivery.
Watch for choral response drills locked to a sequence; that pattern flags DI rather than casual direct teaching.
Classroom vignette: peers recite the same modeled sentence on cue, then the next scripted item appears.
Never confuse any clear oral explanation with the branded Direct Instruction curriculum model.
nearMiss: When a scripted lesson fails, check whether you ran a published Engelmann-Becker program with unison cues, or only loose teacher talk from the front.
Materials can look tight and still not be capital-D Direct Instruction if wording, signals, and correctives are not fixed in a named script.
A front-of-room explanation that never uses choral response frames is lowercase teacher-led teaching, not the branded DI package.
Ask: published script with prescribed lines, or any clear oral explanation? Only the former earns the capital-DI label.
Fixing slides helps only after you know which object you have: general di versus Engelmann and Becker's scripted DI.

items.why: I do, we do, you do - responsibility shifts from teacher to learner across three phases.
faces: I do, then we do, then you do. Teacher shows one fully worked problem, then solves with the class, then students solve alone.
I do models the skill fully before any shared attempt begins.
We do shares the work so the learner still has scaffolding beside them.
You do hands the whole task over only after modeled and guided passes.
Ask which phase owns the cognitive load: teacher alone, joint, or student alone.
Unlike dumping practice first, release moves responsibility across three explicit handoffs.
If peers still need whispered prompts mid-task, they are still in the guided middle stage.
This is not one long lecture then sink-or-swim homework; stages are ordered on purpose.
Student watches a worked example, co-solves a twin item, then attempts a solo clone.
Tool vignette: tutor UI greys out student input until the model step finishes playing.
Decoder line: model, then jointly construct, then independent performance.
Homework only after the third stage matches the intended release sequence.
Scaffold fades as ownership shifts from instructor demonstration toward learner autonomy.
nearMiss: Guidance is not one knob labeled expert-or-novice; it moves across three handoffs: teacher models, class co-solves, then solo work.
A discovery-heavy unit still needs an I-do phase before we-do and you-do, not a single expertise dial turned once.
Watch who owns the cognitive load now: instructor alone, joint scaffold, or learner alone across ordered stages.
Homework after a long lecture without a guided middle pass skips the release sequence, even if the learner is advanced.
Unlike arguing how much freedom experts deserve, this design names model, then shared attempt, then independent performance.

items.why: Voluntary behavior shaped by what follows it. Consequences steer chosen acts.
faces: shape voluntary behavior by what happens after it. Reward closer and closer versions of the target action until the full action appears.
Shape the target by reinforcing closer and closer approximations, not waiting for perfection.
Successive approximations build a complex act one reinforced step at a time.
Ask what tiny improvement just earned the consequence that nudges the next try.
Unlike pairing a neutral cue with an unconditioned stimulus, this path strengthens emitted acts.
If the learner never produces the full skill yet, still reinforce the nearest reachable form.
This is not classical pairing of bell and food; consequences follow voluntary responses.
Student types a half-correct regex, gets a point, then stretches toward the full pattern.
Tool vignette: badge unlocks only when each partial gesture passes the shaping ladder.
Decoder: emitted behavior, then consequence that raises or lowers that behavior's future rate.
Chores completed unlock phone time only after the approximation meets today's bar.
Watch rate of the same voluntary act climb when desirable outcomes follow it reliably.
Practice schedules can thin once the shaped response holds without every trial rewarded.
nearMiss: A bell rings and a treat follows a typed answer; what matters is the treat after the voluntary click, not the bell pairing itself.
Shape closer approximations of a raised hand by consequences that follow the act, not by attaching a reflex to a cue.
Rate of an emitted response climbs when desirable outcomes trail that response, even if a classroom chime co-occurs.
Ask what voluntary move just earned the point. The contingency after the act, not an automatic drool to a tone, steers learning here.
Unlike transferring an involuntary reaction to a new signal, this path strengthens chosen behavior by what happens next.

items.why: Pair stimuli until an automatic response transfers. Involuntary association, not chosen acts.
faces: pair two stimuli until an automatic response transfers. Ring a bell with food until the bell alone makes the dog drool; tests can pair with stress the same way.
Bell rings with food enough times that the bell alone later triggers salivation.
Pair a neutral classroom cue with an already strong stimulus until the cue borrows the reaction.
Ask which previously neutral signal now elicits the response without the original trigger.
Unlike shaping voluntary acts with consequences, this binds an automatic response to a new cue.
If test rooms always co-occur with panic physiology, the room itself can later spark anxiety.
This is not praise after a correct answer; the pairing itself transfers the reflex.
Student feels stomach drop when the proctor login screen appears after many timed drills.
Tool vignette: soft chime always precedes a shock demo until the chime alone raises heart rate.
Decoder: conditioned stimulus predicts unconditioned stimulus; response becomes conditioned.
Exam smell of dry-erase markers starts racing pulse after repeated high-stakes pairings.
Neutral tone plus food, repeated, yields tone-driven anticipation without food present.
Automatic bodily reactions hitch to signals that never caused them before the pairing history.
nearMiss: Points flash after each correct click, yet the gut drop when the login screen alone appears traces pairing with prior stress, not shaping of the click.
A chime always precedes a shock demo until the chime alone raises heart rate; that is cue-to-reflex transfer, not reinforced voluntary approximations.
Praise follows homework, but exam-room smell racing the pulse after repeated high-stakes pairings is automatic association, not consequence shaping.
Ask which previously neutral signal now elicits the bodily reaction without the original trigger. That hitch is pairing, not operant ladders.
Unlike reinforcing successive voluntary forms, this binds an involuntary response to a new cue through repeated co-occurrence.

items.why: Add something liked; behavior goes up.
faces: add something liked so the behavior goes up. Give praise or food after the desired action.
Praise lands right after the desired act so that act becomes more likely next time.
Add a pleasant outcome following good performance; the behavior rate should climb.
Ask did something liked get delivered, and did the target behavior increase afterward?
Unlike removing an aversive, this path delivers an appetitive consequence after the act.
If stars appear on the dashboard only when the quiz is correct, that addition is the reinforcer.
This is not taking dessert away; something valued is presented, not stripped.
Student hears specific praise for citing a source, then cites sources more often.
Tool vignette: green badge plus points grant after each clean commit message.
Decoder: rate goes up because a pleasant thing was added contingent on the response.
Extra playtime arrives after homework finishes on time, raising on-time completions.
Warm verbal approval follows the raised hand, and raising hands becomes more frequent.
Never label added praise as punishment just because it follows a school rule.
nearMiss: Phone freeze ends after chores, but the climb in chore rate came from stars and praise added after each finished job, not from lifting the freeze.
Seatbelt beep stops on buckle, yet the behavior that rose was the one that earned an added badge, not the one that only escaped noise.
Add a liked outcome after the target act so that act becomes more common; escape from an aversive is a different cell.
Ask: was something pleasant delivered, and did the wanted behavior go up? Delivery of a treat, not removal of a hassle, is the tell.
Unlike turning off a nag to strengthen an act, this path presents an appetitive consequence contingent on the response.

items.why: Remove something disliked; behavior goes up. Still reinforcement, not punishment.
faces: remove something disliked so the behavior goes up. Turn off a phone time-limit after chores are done. This increases the chore behavior; it is not punishment.
Phone limit lifts once chores finish, so finishing chores rises to escape the restriction.
Remove an aversive state right after the desired act; that removal strengthens the act.
Ask was something unpleasant taken away, and did the wanted behavior become more common?
Unlike adding praise, the consequence here is escape or avoidance of a disliked condition.
If seatbelt beeping stops only when the buckle clicks, clicking is reinforced by silence.
This is not dessert confiscation; an aversive ends, a pleasant is not stripped for misbehavior.
Student clears the overdue queue so the red banner disappears, then clears queues faster next week.
Tool vignette: nagging notification vanishes the moment the nightly backup completes.
Decoder: rate goes up because an aversive was removed contingent on the response.
Chore chart complete ends the weekend phone freeze, making chore completion more reliable.
Alarm stops only after the problem set uploads, training prompt uploads to silence it.
Escape from a noxious condition, not gift of a treat, is what powers this increase.
nearMiss: Dessert vanishes after an outburst, but the chore rate rose because the phone limit lifted when chores finished: remove disliked, behavior up.
Gaming time is cut for skipped homework, yet buckling rises when the beep stops: escape from an aversive strengthens the buckle, not loss of a treat.
Remove something unpleasant right after the desired act so that act becomes more common; stripping a liked privilege is the other move.
Ask: was an aversive taken away, and did the wanted behavior increase? Silence after the nag ends is reinforcement, not punishment.
Unlike docking recess for a shove, ending a noxious condition contingent on the response raises the response rate.

items.why: Add something disliked; behavior goes down.
faces: add something disliked so the behavior goes down. Add extra chores after the unwanted action.
Extra chores pile on after the rule break so that rule break becomes less likely.
Add an aversive consequence following the unwanted act; expect the act's rate to fall.
Ask was something disliked delivered, and did the problem behavior drop afterward?
Unlike removing dessert, this path presents an unpleasant addition, not a withdrawal of a treat.
If late work triggers mandatory weekend lab time, that added burden is the punisher.
This is not lifting a phone ban for good behavior; something aversive is applied after misuse.
Student talks over peers and receives additional cleanup duty, then interrupts less.
Tool vignette: spam filter quarantine plus a stern admin ticket appear after the policy hit.
Decoder: rate goes down because an aversive was added contingent on the response.
Loud corrective buzz follows each off-task click, cutting the off-task click rate.
Required rewrite of the whole post arrives after plagiarism, reducing copy-paste attempts.
Never call added aversives reinforcement just because they are consequences.
nearMiss: Dessert is taken after the outburst, but interrupting fell because extra cleanup duty was piled on: add disliked, behavior down.
Screen time vanishes after late work, yet talking-over peers drops when mandatory weekend lab is added; the added burden is the punisher.
Present an aversive after the unwanted act so its rate falls; withdrawing a privilege is a different contingency.
Ask: was something disliked delivered, and did the problem behavior drop? New chores after the rule break, not lost dessert alone, fit here.
Unlike removing a liked item after misuse, this path adds an unpleasant consequence contingent on the response.

items.why: Remove something liked; behavior goes down.
faces: remove something liked so the behavior goes down. Take away dessert when dinner is unfinished.
Dessert disappears after the outburst so the outburst becomes rarer.
Remove a pleasant privilege following the unwanted act; expect that act's rate to fall.
Ask was something liked taken away, and did the problem behavior decrease?
Unlike adding extra chores, the consequence here is loss of a valued thing, not a new aversive task.
If gaming time is cut when homework is skipped, the removal is the punisher.
This is not ending a phone freeze for completed chores; a liked item is stripped after misuse.
Student loses weekend screen time after late submission, then submits earlier.
Tool vignette: streak badge vanishes from the profile after the integrity flag.
Decoder: rate goes down because a pleasant was removed contingent on the response.
Recess minutes get docked after the shove, and shoving declines.
Shared playlist privileges revoke after the chat flame, cooling the flame rate.
Withdrawal of a reinforcer after misbehavior, not delivery of a treat, defines this cell.
nearMiss: Phone freeze lifts when chores finish and chore rate rises, but shoving fell because recess minutes were docked: remove liked, behavior down.
Alarm silence trains prompt uploads, yet late submissions drop after weekend screen time is stripped; loss of a liked privilege punishes.
Take away something valued after the unwanted act so that act becomes rarer; ending an aversive to raise a good act is the other cell.
Ask: was a pleasant thing removed, and did the problem behavior decrease? Confiscating dessert, not stopping a beep, is the tell.
Unlike escape from a nag that increases the target response, withdrawal of a reinforcer after misbehavior lowers its rate.

items.why: Reinforcement increases behavior; punishment decreases it. Positive=add, negative=remove. Sort up/down first.
faces: reinforcement tries to increase a behavior; punishment tries to decrease it. Positive means add something; negative means take something away. Ask up-or-down first, then add-or-remove.
First decide whether the behavior rate rose or fell, then decide whether something was added or removed.
Upward trend after the consequence signals reinforcement; downward trend signals punishment.
Ask up-or-down before add-or-remove so the four cells stay untangled.
Unlike guessing from how nice the teacher sounds, track rate change as the primary signal.
If the act becomes more common, you are in reinforcement territory regardless of smiles or frowns.
This is not naming by emotion: pleasant-sounding events can still punish if rate drops.
Student decoder card: arrow up equals reinforce, arrow down equals punish, then +/- for add/remove.
Tool vignette: analytics plot the response frequency before labeling the contingency.
Decoder: rate direction first; contingency sign second; never reverse that order.
Praise that somehow suppresses volunteering is punishment by outcome, not reinforcement by tone.
Chore-for-phone-freedom that increases chore rate is reinforcement even if chores feel hard.
Never skip the up/down test when classifying Module 1 consequence types.
nearMiss: Praise lands after a raised hand and hand-raises climb: first note the rate went up, then that something liked was added.
Extra chores after talking-over make interruptions fall: arrow down marks punishment before you classify the add.
Never name the cell from how nice the consequence sounds; sort whether behavior rose or fell, then whether something was added or removed.
A phone-freedom deal that increases chore completion is reinforcement by outcome even if chores feel hard; up/down first.
Decoder card before any vignette: up equals reinforce, down equals punish, then plus/minus for add versus remove.

items.why: Watching only outward acts could not explain abstraction, transfer, or novel solving. The mind had to come back into the story.
faces: behaviorism could not explain abstract ideas, transfer to new problems, or truly novel solving. Watching only outward actions left the mind unexplained.
Abstraction, transfer, and novel problem solving expose limits of stimulus-response accounts.
Tolman-style cognitive maps show organisms learn layouts without continuous external reinforcement.
Ask whether the task needs internal representation, not only reinforced surface responses.
Unlike shaping every overt act, cognitivism posits mental structures that behaviorism sidelined.
If learners solve a never-reinforced variant, pure contingency histories struggle to explain it.
This is not denying consequences matter; it is insisting they cannot cover planning and transfer alone.
Student invents a strategy never explicitly rewarded yet, cracking a strict behaviorist story.
Tool vignette: tutor logs latent knowledge states instead of only click-reward pairs.
Decoder: cracks appear where maps, rules, and generative language outrun overt reinforcement histories.
Chomsky-style productivity arguments press against treating language as mere shaped chains.
Transfer across contexts needs more than matching prior reinforced surface forms.
Novel solving without a shaped exemplar pushes theories toward internal representations.
nearMiss: Shaping closer clicks with points still cannot explain inventing a never-reinforced strategy on a novel variant.
Badge ladders after voluntary acts leave abstraction and transfer unexplained if only outward contingencies are allowed.
A learner solves a problem with no shaped exemplar of that form; watching responses alone cannot cover the leap.
Ask whether the task needs internal representation for planning and transfer, not only reinforced surface responses.
Unlike denying that consequences matter, the claim is that S-R histories cannot alone cover maps, rules, and generative solving.

items.why: Consequence must land right after the behavior. Delayed feedback weakens the pairing.
faces: the consequence must land right after the behavior. Instant right/wrong after each tiny step beats feedback a week later.
Feedback that arrives on the same trial binds consequence to the exact response just made.
Delay lets intervening acts muddy which behavior the consequence belongs to.
Ask how many other responses sat between the act and the outcome.
Unlike end-of-week grade dumps, same-trial signals keep the contingency crisp.
If the badge pops three screens later, learners may credit the wrong click.
This is not about kindness; timing is what keeps the association tight.
Student submits a step and sees correct/incorrect before starting the next step.
Tool vignette: inline green check fires before the next input field unlocks.
Decoder: shorter lag, cleaner credit assignment for the reinforced response.
Class poll reveals answers instantly so each choice still sits in working memory.
Waiting until Friday to mark Tuesday's drill weakens the link Module 1 stresses.
Frame each consequence so the learner can still recall the precise preceding act.
nearMiss: A tutor explains why the step failed, but the Module 1 timing claim is that the outcome must land on the same trial as the act.
Rich rationale after an error helps the model, yet delayed Friday marks for Tuesday drills still muddy which response earned the mark.
Inline green checks before the next field unlocks bind consequence to the exact click just made; lag lets intervening acts steal credit.
Ask how many other responses sat between the behavior and the outcome. Shorter lag, cleaner pairing of act to consequence.
Unlike focusing on how much the message explains, this rule is about when the consequence arrives relative to the response.

items.why: Study thinking in messy everyday settings, not only clean labs.
faces: study memory and perception in messy real life, not only the lab. How people remember in everyday settings, not only clean experiments.
Memory in messy rooms, tools, and social cues differs from lab lists of nonsense syllables.
Real-world remembering leans on environment structure, not only isolated internal stores.
Ask where the knowledge lives: skull alone, or distributed across notes, peers, and places.
Unlike sterile paired-associate drills, ecological views study cognition in situ.
If the student only recalls the formula when standing at the lab bench, context is doing work.
This is not claiming brains are empty; it stresses coupling between mind and setting.
Student navigates campus by landmarks and phone maps rather than pure mental coordinates.
Tool vignette: checklist on the wall carries steps the worker no longer holds verbally.
Decoder: cognition as adaptive activity in an information-rich environment.
Classroom clutter, posters, and peer talk become part of the remembering system.
Field problems recruit perception-action loops that sterile worksheets omit.
Studying only decontextualized items miss how everyday memory actually functions.
nearMiss: Maze-search metaphors fit clean labs, but memory here is studied in messy rooms, landmarks, and phone maps, not only problem-space operators.
Tower puzzles enumerate legal moves; everyday remembering leans on wall checklists, peers, and places as part of the system.
Ask where knowledge lives when the formula returns only at the lab bench: skull alone, or distributed across setting and tools.
Unlike searching an internal state space of operators and goals, this line studies thinking coupled to information-rich environments.
Field problems and campus navigation show cognition as adaptive activity in situ, not sterile paired-associate search alone.

items.why: Build an internal problem picture and search possible moves - problem-space search, not S-R alone.
faces: people build an internal picture of the problem and search possible moves. Think through a maze of mental states, not only react to a stimulus.
Problem space holds states, operators that transform states, and a goal test.
Means-ends analysis picks operators that shrink the gap between now and the goal.
Ask what legal moves exist from the current state toward the desired end state.
Unlike pure association chains, search through an explicit space organizes the account.
If no operator reduces the difference, the solver may set a subgoal first.
This is not freeform brainstorming without structure; operators and goals constrain search.
Student treats algebra as rewriting states until the goal form appears.
Tool vignette: puzzle app enumerates moves and highlights the remaining distance to solved.
Decoder: represent current state, available operators, and goal; then search.
Tower-like tasks make successive states visible while operators flip disks or tokens.
Planning chooses a sequence of operators, not a single reinforced muscle twitch.
Goal-directed search through a defined space is the Module 1 Newell-Simon signature.
nearMiss: Behaviorism's blind spots on transfer are real, yet the signature move here is representing states, operators, and a goal, then searching.
Mind returns to the story not as an essay against S-R, but as means-ends search that shrinks the gap from current state to goal.
Ask what legal moves exist from this state toward the desired end; that operator search is the account, not only that outward acts failed.
Unlike arguing abstraction forced cognitivism, this framework builds an internal problem picture and explores possible transformations.
Algebra as rewriting states until the goal form appears is problem-space search, not merely a critique that reinforcement histories fall short.

items.why: Explain why the answer failed so the mental model updates. Bare wrong/try-again mostly nudges the next click.
faces: saying only “wrong, try again” mainly nudges the next click; saying why it was wrong updates the mental model. Fix the understanding, not just the answer.
Explain why the attempt failed instead of only flashing wrong-try-again.
Information about the underlying rule beats bare correctness labels for building models.
Ask whether the message repairs the misconception or just flags the error.
Unlike behaviorist stamps of right/wrong, cognitivist notes target mental structures.
If the hint names the missing principle, transfer to the next item improves.
This is not endless praise; it is diagnostic content about the reasoning gap.
Student reads which step violated conservation rather than only seeing a red X.
Tool vignette: tutor quotes the broken invariant and offers a contrasting worked case.
Decoder: feedback as knowledge update, not solely as reinforcing contingency.
Wrong-try-again alone leaves the faulty representation intact for the next attempt.
Rich rationale after an error supports revising the internal model of the task.
Prefer explanatory corrective text over opaque binary outcomes when cognition is the goal.
nearMiss: Instant wrong/try-again keeps timing tight, but bare stamps leave the faulty rule intact; name the broken principle so the model updates.
Same-trial marks bind consequence to the click, yet learning the concept needs why the attempt failed, not only that it failed now.
Ask whether the message repairs the misconception or only flags the error before the next input unlocks.
Unlike prioritizing lag alone, diagnostic content about the reasoning gap revises the internal representation of the task.
A red X that arrives immediately still mostly nudges the next click; explanatory corrective text targets the understanding.

items.why: Intrinsic=content hardness; extraneous=junk design; germane=useful thinking. Cut clutter; sequence hard ideas.
faces: intrinsic is how hard the content is; extraneous is useless clutter; germane is useful thinking work. Remove decorative junk and sequence hard ideas.
Intrinsic load tracks how hard the material is given the learner's current schemas.
Extraneous load is waste from poor design that does not help schema building.
Germane load is the productive effort spent constructing and automating schemas.
Ask which of the three buckets the current animation or narration is filling.
Unlike treating all effort as good, sort demand into intrinsic, extraneous, and germane.
If decorative side quests consume working memory, that cost is extraneous.
This is not a single fatigue meter; three qualitatively different loads matter.
Student struggles because element interactivity is high, not because the UI is noisy.
Tool vignette: redesign removes split attention so extraneous demand falls.
Decoder: intrinsic from content complexity; extraneous from design fluff; germane from useful processing.
Working memory limits make unmanaged extraneous detail crowd out learning work.
Raise germane processing only after cutting avoidable extraneous demands.
nearMiss: A talking-head pane can steal attention, but the load claim sorts demand into intrinsic content hardness, extraneous junk, and germane useful work.
Dropping a corner webcam may help, yet the deeper move is cutting decorative clutter and sequencing hard ideas across the three load types.
Ask which bucket the current animation fills: material complexity, avoidable design waste, or productive schema building.
Unlike a single rule about instructor faces, unmanaged extraneous detail crowds working memory away from germane processing.
Redesign that removes split attention lowers extraneous load even when no face cam was present; classify the three loads first.

items.why: Adding a talking-head face to narration usually does not improve learning and can steal attention.
faces: adding the instructor’s face to a narrated lesson usually does not improve learning. The face rarely adds new information and can steal attention.
Talking-head video of the instructor rarely helps more than the narration plus relevant graphics.
Static instructor face often adds little when the lesson already has spoken words and diagrams.
Ask whether the on-screen person explains anything the visuals and voice do not already cover.
Unlike relevant diagrams of the process, a floating lecturer portrait is usually decorative.
If replacing the talking head with a labeled animation improves learning, the head was surplus.
This is not a ban on all video; it targets redundant instructor likeness without instructional role.
Student watches a corner webcam while a circuit diagram does the real teaching work.
Tool vignette: A/B test drops the face cam and keeps voice-over with schematics.
Decoder: Image Principle favors relevant graphics over ornamental talking heads.
Narration plus meaningful visuals beat narration plus an unrelated smiling instructor pane.
Camera-on presence without pointing to structure tends to waste limited attention.
Prefer process imagery that maps to the explanation over continuous face footage.
nearMiss: Cute unrelated explosions waste attention, but the face claim is narrower: a talking-head likeness usually adds no new information and can steal focus.
Strip seductive stock footage and still test whether the instructor portrait helps more than narration plus relevant diagrams.
Ask whether the on-screen person explains anything the voice and process graphics do not already cover; ornamental faces rarely do.
Unlike cutting every interesting extra, this rule targets redundant instructor likeness without an instructional pointing role.
A/B tests that drop the face cam and keep labeled animations often match or beat continuous smiling-pane video.

items.why: Cute non-teaching visuals can hurt learning by wasting limited attention.
faces: visuals that do not teach the idea can hurt learning. Cute unrelated animations waste limited attention.
Seductive details that are interesting but irrelevant hurt learning more than they help.
Cut anecdotes, jokes, and fancy extras that do not support the instructional goal.
Ask whether each clip or fact is needed for the objective or only for entertainment.
Unlike enriching with germane examples, seductive add-ons siphon working memory.
If a cool explosion video is unrelated to the circuit rule, coherence says remove it.
This is not anti-engagement; it is anti-irrelevant engagement that dilutes the message.
Student remembers the funny meme from the slide and forgets the theorem beside it.
Tool vignette: editor strips stock footage that never appears in the assessment.
Decoder: Coherence Principle equals delete interesting-but-off-target material.
Extra background music with lyrics can act as seductive auditory clutter.
Keep only words and graphics that advance the learning objective.
Trim decorative stories even when learners rate them as highly enjoyable.
nearMiss: Corner webcam of the lecturer rarely helps, but coherence cuts any non-teaching extra: jokes, memes, and fancy clips off the objective.
Face-on-video can distract, yet the broader delete rule removes interesting-but-irrelevant details even when no talking head appears.
Ask whether each clip or anecdote is needed for the learning goal or only for entertainment; keep only what advances the objective.
Unlike a ban on instructor likeness alone, seductive details that learners enjoy can still siphon working memory from the theorem.
Trim decorative stories and lyric-backed music that never appear in the assessment, not merely decide whether a face pane stays.

items.why: After performance, judge how it went and why. Part of self-regulated learning.
faces: after the work, judge how it went and why. Plan before, do the work, then ask what caused the result. SRL = self-regulated learning.
After the attempt, pause and ask what worked, what failed, and what to change next time.
Plan the approach, do the work, then look back; skipping the look-back leaves the loop broken.
Unlike blind repetition, this step turns experience into a revised strategy for the next round.
If the session ends without a check on process, the plan-do cycle never becomes regulation.
Ask what you would do differently before starting another identical drill.
This is not scoring yourself on talent; it is reviewing moves so the next plan improves.
Write one concrete tweak after each practice block instead of only noting the score.
Tool tip: a short after-action note beats rereading notes with no process review.
Decoder: plan, act, then judge the process; the third beat is the regulation piece.
Homework done, still no habit change? The missing beat is looking back on how you worked.
Catch yourself mid-week and name one strategy to keep and one to drop.
Nightly review of study moves (not just grades) closes the self-regulated loop.
nearMiss: Notes feel smooth after another pass, yet the useful move is pausing to judge what caused the last attempt to succeed or fail, not trusting the easy skim.
A practice quiz goes blank and the warm reread glow tempted confidence; close the loop by naming why the plan worked or broke before the next drill.
Familiar highlighter pages look like knowing under study stress, but the SRL beat is after-action review of process, not ease of reading the same paragraph again.
When the chapter slides by fluently, ask what strategy produced the score you just earned rather than treating page-turn comfort as mastery.
Study surface shared with false familiarity: still land on looking back at how you worked and why, not on how easy the reread felt.

items.why: Ease of rereading feels like knowing but is not recall. Practice tests expose the gap.
faces: feeling smooth after rereading is not the same as being able to recall it. Notes feel familiar, then the quiz is blank; a practice quiz exposes that.
Rereading feels smooth, so confidence jumps even when recall under pressure is still weak.
Smooth page-turning tricks the brain into thinking the material is locked in.
Unlike a practice quiz, passive review rarely exposes what you cannot yet retrieve.
If the text looks familiar, do not trust that feeling until a blank-page check fails or passes.
Ask whether you can produce the answer without looking, not whether the words look known.
This is not real mastery; familiarity from rereads is a different signal than retrieval.
Swap the highlighter pass for a closed-notes quiz to puncture false confidence.
Tool check: a short practice quiz beats another fluent skim of the same chapter.
Decoder: ease of reading is not evidence of durable learning.
Highlight glow and easy rereads can hide empty retrieval until the exam.
Catch the warm glow of reread comfort and treat it as a warning, not a green light.
Practice retrieval first; only then decide whether the material is actually learned.
nearMiss: After the block, a learner writes what to change next time, yet the trap that still fools them is mistaking smooth rereading for locked-in recall.
Plan-do-judge notes sit in the margin while the highlighter pass still feels like knowing; familiarity from another skim is not retrieval under pressure.
SRL look-back can be sincere and still leave a blank quiz if confidence came from easy page-turning rather than producing answers closed-book.
Reflection prompts ask why the drill went poorly; the deeper miss is that prior reread comfort never proved the material was actually recallable.
Shared after-study scene with process review, but the claim lands on ease-of-reading confidence that fails when the page is gone.

items.why: Stress can use up the attention needed to notice you are lost. Monitoring needs spare capacity.
faces: stress can use up the attention you need to notice you are lost. After the pressure drops, you suddenly see what you missed.
Stress burns the bandwidth you need to notice whether your strategy is working.
High load shrinks the mental space used to watch your own progress mid-task.
Unlike calm practice, panic leaves little room to catch a bad approach early.
If anxiety spikes, expect weaker self-checks even when content knowledge is fine.
Ask whether overload, not ignorance, is why you stopped noticing mistakes.
This is not a knowledge gap alone; monitoring itself gets crowded out under pressure.
Lower the threat first so you can still track what is and is not working.
Tool design that piles timers and threats can erase the learner's self-watch.
Decoder: monitoring needs spare capacity; stress eats that spare capacity.
Deadline panic can make a skilled student stop noticing their own errors.
Catch rising stress and protect a bit of attention for process checks.
Quiet the threat so judgment of your own learning can come back online.
nearMiss: Reread pages feel familiar under a ticking timer, yet the real failure is stress eating the spare attention needed to notice you are lost mid-task.
Smooth skimming and panic arrive together on exam night; what drops first is the bandwidth to watch whether the strategy still works.
False knowing from easy notes can co-occur with anxiety, but the distinctive hit is overloaded monitoring, not the familiarity illusion alone.
Ask whether rising threat, not just another fluent chapter pass, is why process checks went offline until the pressure eased.
Shared study-and-quiz surface with fluency traps; land on capacity for self-watch getting crowded out when stress spikes.

items.why: Learn by joining real activity beside more experienced people - not only hearing a talk about it.
faces: learn by watching and joining real activity beside more experienced people. Help cook the meal; do not only hear a talk about cooking.
Cook beside an expert so real kitchen moves transfer while help is still nearby.
Side-by-side authentic work with a more skilled other, not a lecture about cooking.
Unlike solo trial-and-error, joint activity lets the novice join real practice with support.
If the expert only demos from afar, the learner never shares the actual task space.
Ask to join the real activity with fading help rather than watch a slide about it.
This is not pure lecture; learning happens while doing the valued task together.
Stand next to the expert and take a real turn with coaching still in reach.
Tool analogy: a shared workspace with an expert beats a video of the expert alone.
Decoder: participate in the real practice with guidance, not only hear about it.
Kitchen apprentice model: join the work, get support, then carry more of the load.
Catch the difference between hearing a recipe and cooking while coached.
Shared authentic tasks with an expert nearby beat isolated textbook drills.
nearMiss: A newcomer takes a real edge task in the kitchen community, but the claim here is joining the valued activity beside a more experienced cook, not the periphery-to-center arc.
Legitimate micro-jobs at the group's margin look similar; this path is side-by-side authentic practice with an expert still in reach, not membership trajectory alone.
Community onboarding gives peripheral roles that matter, yet Rogoff's move is participate in the real work while coached, not only map who sits at the edge.
Ask to cook the meal with help nearby rather than only track how far from the center the first tasks sit.
Shared apprentice kitchen scene with LPP; land on joint authentic activity beside expertise, not the edge-then-inward story.

items.why: Newcomers do real low-stakes work at the edge of a community, then move toward the center.
faces: a newcomer does real but low-stakes work at the edge of a group, then moves toward the center. First do simple real tasks the group actually needs, then harder ones.
Start on the edge of a real community with small authentic tasks that still matter.
Peripheral but genuine roles let newcomers contribute before they own the center.
Unlike fake worksheet communities, these tasks belong to the real practice of the group.
If the first jobs are fake busywork, newcomers never enter authentic participation.
Ask for a real though limited role, not a simulation disconnected from the community.
This is not full membership on day one; it is legitimate work at the periphery.
Give newcomers authentic edge tasks that the community actually uses.
Tool for onboarding: assign a real micro-task the group cares about, then grow scope.
Decoder: legitimate peripheral participation means real work, edge role, growing inward.
Newcomer status with genuine tasks beats spectator status with no stake.
Catch fake participation: if the task never touches community practice, it is not this.
Edge authenticity first; centrality grows as competence and trust grow.
nearMiss: Cook beside an expert so kitchen moves transfer with help in reach, yet the Lave and Wenger claim is real low-stakes edge work that later moves toward the center.
Side-by-side authentic turns look like guided cooking; the tell is legitimate peripheral roles that the community actually uses, then growing inward.
Joint activity with a skilled other can be the surface, while the distinctive path is newcomer status with genuine tasks before centrality.
Hearing a recipe while standing next to the chef is not enough; assign a real though limited community task and grow scope as competence grows.
Shared cook-beside surface with guided participation; land on edge authenticity first, then movement toward full membership.

items.why: More than one valid way to reason or represent. Do not force a single style as the only correct one.
faces: allow more than one valid way to reason or represent an idea. Do not assume one style of thinking is the only correct one.
Multiple reasoning styles can be valid; one classroom norm is not the only logic.
Different communities may prize different ways of arguing and still be rigorous.
Unlike a single correct discourse style, several cultural patterns can solve well.
If a student reasons differently, check whether the style is other-valid, not merely wrong.
Ask whether the mismatch is deficit or a different valued form of sense-making.
This is not anything-goes relativism; it is recognizing plural valid reasoning paths.
Treat alternate discourse patterns as possible strengths before labeling them errors.
Tool designers who hard-code one talk style can misread other cultural logics.
Decoder: variation across cultures can mean multiple acceptable reasoning moves.
Classroom norms that fit one group may silence another equally sound approach.
Catch the bias that only one talk pattern counts as smart.
Plural valid styles; do not equate unfamiliar discourse with weak thinking.
nearMiss: Learners join real kitchen work beside an expert, yet the equity claim is that more than one reasoning or talk style can still be rigorous and valid.
Joint authentic practice can hide a single-norm bias; honor plural sense-making paths rather than treating one classroom discourse as the only smart form.
Apprenticeship scenes invite participation, but the miss is forcing one representation style while another cultural pattern solves equally well.
Ask whether the mismatch is deficit or a different valued form of arguing, not only whether the novice stood next to the expert.
Shared participate-with-others surface; land on multiple acceptable styles, not the joint-activity definition alone.

items.why: ZPD is the zone (gap); scaffolding is temporary help inside that zone. Where versus what support.
faces: ZPD is the gap between alone and with help; scaffolding is the temporary support inside that gap. Zone of proximal development = the zone; scaffolding = the help in the zone.
Zone is the gap between solo and helped success; scaffolding is the temporary help that fades.
Unlike scaffolding, the zone names where learning sits, not the supports themselves.
If help never thins out, you may still be in a useful zone but you are not scaffolding well.
Ask whether you are naming the performance gap or describing the fading supports.
This is not the same construct twice; one is the target range, the other is how help withdraws.
Map the zone first, then design supports that leave once independence appears.
Tool scaffolds belong inside a zone and should disappear; the zone itself is not a worksheet.
Decoder: ZPD equals range of doable-with-help; scaffolding equals fading assistance.
Permanent answer keys are not scaffolding even if the task sits in a productive zone.
Catch the mix-up: calling any hint a zone, or calling a zone the fading help.
Range versus fading aid: keep those two labels pointed at different things.
Sibling check: zone describes capacity with help; scaffolding describes help that goes away.
nearMiss: Alone the proof stalls and with a worked example it finishes; that middle band is the zone, while scaffolding names the temporary help that should fade inside it.
Can-with-help success marks the instructional target range; fading worksheets and cues are the supports, not another name for the same gap.
If help never thins, you may still sit in a useful zone but you are not scaffolding well. Zone equals where; scaffold equals withdrawing aid.
Ask whether you are pointing at the solo-versus-helped performance gap or describing the fading assists that live inside that gap.
Shared with-help band surface with ZPD; land on the distinction between the zone and temporary support that goes away.

items.why: Success means actually understanding, not looking better than others.
faces: success means actually understanding, not looking better than others. “I got it” beats “I looked smart.”
Aim to get better at the skill, not to look smarter than peers in the moment.
Progress on the craft beats protecting an image of being already smart.
Unlike performance goals that chase looking able, this goal chases real improvement.
If a hard problem threatens status, mastery still treats struggle as useful data.
Ask whether the target is growth on the task or applause for looking competent.
This is not about proving talent; it is about improving competence over time.
Choose hard practice that builds skill even when it risks looking imperfect.
Tool feedback that praises cleverness over progress can pull learners off mastery.
Decoder: mastery orients to getting better; looking-smart orients to image.
Struggle on a stretch problem is welcome when the goal is skill, not status.
Catch ego goals that trade learning for appearing already good.
Growth on the skill outranks looking impressive after one flashy success.
nearMiss: The same dunk attempt can chase a highlight reel or dodge a blooper, yet mastery still measures success as actually understanding, not looking impressive.
Performance approach hunts Top-10 glory while avoidance ducks the fail tape; the mastery goal ignores both and asks whether the skill itself improved.
Highlight and blooper motives can share one attempt; choose hard practice that builds competence even when it risks looking imperfect.
Ask whether the target is growth on the craft or applause for making the reel / not making the blooper reel.
Shared sports-reel surface with ESPN framing; land on understand-versus-look-smart, not approach-highlight versus avoid-blooper.

items.why: Performance-approach hunts the highlight reel; performance-avoidance dodges the blooper reel - often on the same attempt.
faces: performance-approach tries to make the highlight reel; performance-avoidance tries to avoid the blooper reel. The same dunk attempt can become either.
Show the highlight reel of strong moves, not only the blooper of what went wrong.
Top-10 style review celebrates what worked; Not-Top-10 only loops the mistakes.
Unlike endless blooper reels, a highlight pass teaches the successful pattern.
If feedback only replays failures, learners miss models of what good looks like.
Ask for examples of strong performance before dwelling on every miss.
This is not ignoring errors; it is balancing critique with visible successful moves.
Replay the good play so the class can copy the structure of success.
Tool default that only flags wrongs is a blooper channel, not a Top-10 channel.
Decoder: highlight effective moves; do not only loop the fails.
Classroom critique that never shows wins trains avoidance more than skill.
Catch Not-Top-10 culture: constant bloopers with no model of the highlight.
Balance the reel: include successful attempts beside the corrections.
nearMiss: Wanting to really get it rather than look smart can still sit beside a dunk that is either hunting the highlight reel or dodging the blooper reel.
Mastery talk about understanding the move does not erase the performance split: approach seeks Top-10 glory; avoidance only tries not to be Not-Top-10.
A stretch problem framed as growth can still be played as make-the-reel versus never-miss-on-camera; same attempt, two performance motives.
Ask whether the motive on this try is appear on the highlight pass or stay off the blooper pass, not only whether deep understanding is valued.
Shared look-smart-versus-learn surface with mastery; land on performance-approach highlight versus performance-avoidance blooper.

items.why: Message that feeling out of place is normal and temporary can raise motivation and grades.
faces: tell students that feeling out of place is normal and temporary. That message can raise motivation and grades.
A brief message that doubt is common and temporary can keep people in the course.
Hearing that struggle does not mean you do not fit reduces early exit risk.
Unlike permanent-outsider framing, temporary-doubt framing protects persistence.
If early worry says you do not belong, treat that feeling as common and passing.
Ask whether the story in your head is fixed exclusion or a normal early wobble.
This is not empty cheerleading; it is naming belonging uncertainty as temporary.
Normalize early doubt so students stay long enough for competence to grow.
Tool onboarding copy that says many feel this way at first can change stay-or-leave.
Decoder: belonging intervention frames doubt as temporary, not destiny.
First-week isolation feelings fade when the message says they are common and brief.
Catch the permanent-outsider story and replace it with a temporary-doubt story.
Short belonging cues beat silence when newcomers wonder if they fit.
nearMiss: Choice, growing skill, and peer ties feed drive, yet the Walton and Cohen move is a brief message that feeling out of place is common and temporary.
Autonomy-competence-relatedness designs can still miss early exit risk if nobody names first-week outsider doubt as normal and passing.
Motivation triad supports help, but the distinctive intervention is reframing I-do-not-fit as temporary, not destiny.
Ask whether onboarding copy says many feel this wobble at first, not only whether the system offers voice, progress, and connection.
Shared motivation-support surface with self-determination; land on the out-of-place-is-temporary message, not the full needs triad.

items.why: Motivation needs autonomy, competence, and relatedness.
faces: motivation needs autonomy, competence, and relatedness. Meaningful choice, a sense I can do this, and connection to people.
Motivation rises when autonomy, competence, and relatedness are supported together.
Choice, growing skill, and real connection to others feed sustained drive.
Unlike pure reward control, supporting those three needs builds lasting engagement.
If any of the three needs is crushed, expect motivation to thin even with points.
Ask whether the design offers voice, progress, and belonging to other people.
This is not bribery alone; it is feeding autonomy, competence, and relatedness.
Protect learner choice, clear growth paths, and social ties in the same system.
Tool that only adds badges but removes choice and peer ties misses the triad.
Decoder: autonomy plus competence plus relatedness underpins self-determined drive.
External pressure without those three supports often yields fragile compliance.
Catch designs that score points while starving voice, mastery, or connection.
Triad check: can they choose, get better, and feel linked to others?
nearMiss: A note that early doubt is common and brief can keep people in, yet lasting drive still needs autonomy, competence, and relatedness supported together.
Belonging cues lower exit risk while the Deci and Ryan claim remains: meaningful choice, growing skill, and real connection underwrite motivation.
Temporary-outsider framing helps persistence; check whether the design also feeds voice, progress, and ties, not only a one-time fit message.
Ask whether learners can choose, get better, and feel linked to others, even after the first-week belonging note lands.
Shared stay-or-leave motivation surface with belonging; land on the autonomy-competence-relatedness triad.

items.why: Systems struggled more with darker-skinned faces; captive users take uneven harm.
faces: the systems struggled more with darker-skinned faces. People forced to use the tool get uneven harm.
Darker-skinned faces trigger more false fails in some face-detection proctor stacks.
Camera identity checks can misread melanin-rich skin as a violation or no-face.
Unlike fair lighting for all, biased detectors punish some faces more often.
If the proctor tool flags no face, check demographic bias before blaming the student.
Ask whether the fail rate tracks skin tone rather than actual cheating.
This is not neutral tech; face models can fail unevenly across skin tones.
Audit proctor false rejects by demographics before trusting every lockout.
Tool bias: remote face match that drops darker faces creates unfair exam blocks.
Decoder: darker-skinned students hit higher false-negative face detection.
Exam lockouts from bad face detect can be a fairness bug, not misconduct.
Catch skin-tone linked fail spikes in the proctoring logs.
Fairness review of face models belongs next to any remote-proctor rollout.
nearMiss: Softer critique by demographic group is another fairness bug, but this stack's tell is face detection that fails more on darker-skinned faces and locks exams unfairly.
AI tutors may withhold hard corrections for some identities; here the captive-user harm is camera identity checks misreading melanin-rich skin as no-face.
Uneven EdTech by group shares the ethics surface; land on proctor false rejects tracking skin tone rather than actual cheating.
Ask whether the fail spike is biased face match before blaming misconduct, not whether feedback tone was gentler for a labeled group.
Shared demographic-harm surface with AI feedback bias; land on darker-skin face-fail in remote proctoring.

items.why: Girls and underrepresented minorities got less critical feedback - softer is not equal help.
faces: girls and underrepresented minorities got less critical feedback. Softer comments are not equal help.
Some AI tutors soften critique for girls and URM students and leave gaps unfixed.
Gentler tone to protected groups can withhold the hard correction they still need.
Unlike equal rigor, demographic-conditioned softness creates uneven feedback quality.
If the model praises more and corrects less for some groups, learning equity drops.
Ask whether critique strength tracks identity labels instead of work quality alone.
This is not kindness that helps; uneven soft feedback can stall skill growth.
Demand the same precise correction for every demographic when the error is the same.
Tool audit: compare critique severity across gender and URM labels on matched work.
Decoder: softer AI critique for girls or URM can mean less useful feedback.
Matched essays getting unequal hardness of critique is a demographic bias signal.
Catch praise-heavy, fix-light responses aimed at some identities only.
Equal diagnostic bite across groups beats identity-tuned softness that hides errors.
nearMiss: Proctor cameras that drop darker faces create uneven exam harm, yet this claim is matched work getting less critical AI critique for girls and underrepresented minorities.
Face-detect lockouts are a sibling fairness story; here softer, praise-heavy comments leave the same errors unfixed for some groups.
Demographic bias in required tools shares the scene; land on unequal diagnostic bite in automated feedback, not camera identity fails.
Ask whether critique severity tracks identity labels on identical essays, not whether the webcam called no-face on darker skin.
Shared unfair-by-group EdTech surface with remote proctoring; land on less critical feedback by demographic.

items.why: Poorly designed EdTech helps the already-ahead first; the gap can widen early.
faces: poorly designed tech helps students who are already ahead first. The gap grows before the tool helps everyone.
Learners already ahead get more of the next boost, widening the gap further.
Early advantage attracts more help, tools, and attention than late starters receive.
Unlike equal allocation, gains compound toward those who started stronger.
If enrichment goes first to the top scorers, the already-ahead pull further ahead.
Ask who receives the scarce tutor time: those thriving or those still catching up.
This is not neutral merit alone; prior lead often buys the next opportunity.
Watch designs that feed the strongest first and starve the ones behind.
Tool routing that prioritizes high performers recreates richer-get-richer dynamics.
Decoder: already-ahead students capture first claim on new resources.
Small early leads plus preferential support snowball into large later gaps.
Catch enrichment pipelines that only open for those already winning.
Resource flow to the front of the pack is the classic widening pattern.
nearMiss: VAK style quizzes promise personalization, but poorly designed tech still routes the next boost to learners already ahead and widens the early gap.
Visual-auditory-kinesthetic matching is a myth on the same equity beat; the Reich pattern is prior lead capturing first claim on scarce help and tools.
Talk of individual differences can hide richer-get-richer routing: enrichment opens for top scorers while late starters wait.
Ask who receives the scarce tutor time first, those thriving or those catching up, not which modality box a style inventory assigned.
Shared personalization-and-gaps surface with learning-styles; land on already-ahead gains compounding first.

items.why: Matching teaching to VAK styles is a myth. Real differences: prior knowledge, language, access, disability.
faces: matching teaching to a preferred “style” is a myth. What actually differs is prior knowledge, language, access, and disability.
VAK matching is a myth; prior knowledge, language, access, and disability matter more.
Sorting students into visual/auditory/kinesthetic boxes does not improve learning.
Unlike style labels, real barriers are background knowledge, language, access, disability.
If a design only swaps modalities to match a style quiz, it misses the real levers.
Ask about prior knowledge and access before buying a learning-styles inventory.
This is not evidence-based personalization; VAK matching lacks solid support.
Drop the style quiz and diagnose knowledge gaps, language load, and access barriers.
Tool that claims visual-learner mode while ignoring disability access is misaimed.
Decoder: ditch VAK matching; attend to prior knowledge, language, access, disability.
Modality preference feelings are not a license to ignore evidence on what works.
Catch the myth that teaching to a declared style unlocks learning.
Real equity levers beat decorating lessons for a self-reported style type.
nearMiss: Already-ahead students may capture new tools first, yet matching teaching to visual, auditory, or kinesthetic labels remains a myth without solid support.
Matthew-style widening gaps matter; still drop the style quiz and attend to prior knowledge, language, access, and disability as the real levers.
Resource flow to the front of the pack can co-occur with a VAK inventory that never improves learning; modality preference is not the equity fix.
Ask about background knowledge and access barriers before buying a learning-styles sorter, even when early advantage looks unfair.
Shared who-benefits equity surface with Matthew effect; land on VAK matching myth and real differences that actually matter.

items.why: Measure this student's learning for a grade or feedback - one person's reading.
faces: measure this student’s learning to give a grade or feedback. Read one person’s heart rate.
One student meter: how much did this learner know or can do on the target?
Score the person against learning goals, not the whole program's worth.
Unlike judging a tool or curriculum, this judges an individual learner's standing.
If the question is what this student achieved, you are in student-level measurement.
Ask how strong this one learner is on the outcomes, not whether the app should ship.
This is not a program verdict; it is a reading on one learner's performance.
Use a quiz or rubric to locate one student on the skill scale.
Tool report card for a person is assessment; a pilot study of the tool is not.
Decoder: assessment meters one student; keep the target as that learner.
Individual competence check sits here; system-quality judgment sits elsewhere.
Catch the swap: calling a course-wide tool review a student score.
Sibling-safe: student meter only; leave program or tool judgment to evaluation.
nearMiss: Heart-rate readings can compare two workout plans, yet this meter asks how much this one learner knows or can do on the target.
Program pilots use the same quizzes to judge a tool; here the object is one student's standing for grade or feedback, not whether the curriculum should ship.
Shared measures sit on both sides; land on the person-level reading, not the system-level verdict about the design.
Ask what Alice scored on the outcome, not whether the app helped the class as a whole.
Same score sheet as evaluation's evidence; the claim is one-student measurement only.

items.why: Use those measures to judge whether a tool or curriculum works - the design, not one grade alone.
faces: use those measures to judge whether a tool or curriculum works. Compare two workout plans using the same heart-rate readings.
Judge the program or tool: did the intervention work as a design, not one kid's score?
Appraise the curriculum, platform, or policy against its claimed aims.
Unlike a single learner's meter, this verdict is about the system or product.
If the question is whether the tool helps learners in general, that is program judgment.
Ask whether the design should continue, change, or ship, not what one student scored.
This is not one person's grade; it is a judgment of the intervention or product.
Run a study of the tool's impact across users to decide if the design holds up.
Tool pilots and course reviews belong here; a midterm for Alice does not.
Decoder: evaluation judges the program or tool, not a lone student snapshot.
System-level worth check sits here; individual competence checks sit elsewhere.
Catch the swap: treating one exam score as proof the whole platform works.
Sibling-safe: program or tool verdict only; leave the one-student meter to assessment.
nearMiss: Alice's midterm shows what she can do, yet using those measures to decide if the tool or curriculum works is a different judgment.
One learner's grade is on the sheet; the evaluation question is whether the intervention holds up across users and should continue or change.
Shared quizzes and rubrics supply evidence; land on appraising the program or product, not locating a single student on the skill scale.
Ask whether the design should ship, not what one person scored on Friday's quiz.
Same heart-rate readings as assessment's meter; the claim is judging the workout plan, not one athlete's pulse alone.
